title: Pricing determines your business model: what each price order-of-magnitude implies
summary: Jason Cohen argues price isn't an afterthought but core business design, tied to brand, product, buyer, and go-to-market. He walks through each order of magnitude ($0 to $100,000/mo) and what it forces on support, sales, funding, and product, and says to discuss price in customer interviews.

principles.text: Price is business design, not a late-stage optimization; it shapes product, brand, buyer, and company structure.
principles.quote: Price is not an exercise in maximizing some micro-economic supply/demand curve, slapped post facto onto the product. Rather, it fundamentally determines the nature of the product and the structure of the business that produces it.

principles.text: Talk about price in customer development interviews; price is as much a fit factor as any feature.
principles.quote: Price is as important as any other feature to determine product/market "fit."

principles.text: In interviews, probe cost expectations, who writes the check, who approves, and whether an ROI pitch would be welcomed.
principles.quote: Talk about their expectations of cost, and why, who would write the check, who would need to approve it, whether an ROI argument would be welcomed or scoffed at

principles.text: $100/mo is the sweet spot for bootstrappers: broad B2B market, profitable with 200-300 customers, and you can afford to acquire them.
principles.quote: I love this price zone for bootstrapped companies, because it's low enough that you can address a broad business market, but high enough that you can get nicely profitable with a reasonable, achievable number of customers (e.g. 200-300)

principles.text: At $10/mo you can't afford marketing or sales; reaching $1M/yr takes 8000+ customers and growth is slow, so scaling fast usually needs venture funding.
principles.quote: it takes over 8000 customers to make only $1m/yr in revenue

principles.text: At $1,000/mo you face real buying processes and discount requests, with sales costs like much bigger deals but without the revenue, so profit is hard.
principles.quote: This can be a surprisingly difficult zone to become profitable in, because the sales and marketing motions and engineering costs are the same as for much larger sales, but without the attendant revenue.
